utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, good morning all. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case next on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-30/1-A, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Mladjo Radic, Zoran Zigic and Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I should first find out if the equipment is functioning. Can I be heard in Australia? CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Good evening, Your Honour. My name is Ron Cahill. I am Chief Magistrate of Canberra, Australia. So I hope you can hear me clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cahill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We should, I think, take the opportunity to introduce ourselves as we are a moving institution. Perhaps before the business of the day begins I should introduce this Bench to you. My name is Shahabuddeen. I am presiding. On my right is Vice-President Pocar. On his right is Judge Guney. On my left is Judge Mumba, and on her left is Judge Weinberg de Roca. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Good evening to you all from Australia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I mentioned the communications system, and I am pleased to hear that it is functioning. But may I in the customary way more particularly inquire if I am being heard in a language that they understand by the appellants in this case. Yes? Thank you. Am I being heard also by counsel for the appellants? And by counsel for the Prosecution? And of course by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, so as to have the case properly constituted, may I take the appearances. This morning I received a letter from Mr. Krstan Simic indicating that for one reason or another neither he nor his client, Mr. Kvocka, will be here today. So may I turn to Mr. Mladjo Radic and ask for any appearances on his behalf. Is there any appearance? For Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I am Toma Fila representing Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Any appearances for Mr. Zigic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Slobodan Stojanovic, an attorney from Belgrade, representing Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the appearances for Mr. Prcac. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am Jovan Simic, attorney from Belgrade, representing Mr. Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I would turn to the Prosecution for appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours. Helen Brady appearing on behalf of the Prosecution, and with me Mr. David Re and Ms. Norul Rashid, and our case manager is Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Magistrate, may I put in a word of introduction. We are here today pursuant to orders issued by the Appeals Chamber on 25 June 2004 and 14 July 2004, respectively, to hear the additional evidence of witness KV2 as a Court witness. This has been made possible through the kind cooperation of the authorities of the Commonwealth of Australia. So this Branch thanks the authorities of the Commonwealth of Australia for making these arrangements, and in particular for making your valuable services available, Chief Magistrate. This is, in fact, the first time that the ICTY is, I think, taking evidence by videolink with the participation of a judicial officer assigned by the State in which the evidence is to be given. We believe that it is possible for the Australian regime and the Tribunal's regime to co-exist. We appreciate, Mr. Chief Magistrate, that you have to comply with the Australian law, as stated, I believe, in the International War Crimes Tribunals Act of 1995. I'm glad to say that for our part, we see no reason for supposing that that compliance is at variance with the essentials of our procedures. So I shall now resume the necessary facts. The case on appeal was heard orally during the week 23 to 26 March 2004. Two additional witnesses had been ordered to testify in the appeal brought the appellant Mr. Zigic. One of these did so. The other one, a Court witness, was not available. It was ordered that this witness, Witness KV2, would testify as soon as the necessary arrangements were made. With the courteous cooperation of the Commonwealth of Australia, arrangements have now been made for him to testify by videolink from the Commonwealth. Witness KV2 -- when Witness KV2 testifies -- it was ordered that the Appeals Chamber would hear the evidence of two Prosecution witnesses in rebuttal by the Scheduling Order of 14 July 2004; their testimonies would be taken tomorrow and Wednesday. KV2 is a witness of the Appeals Chamber, as I have said. By orders dated 2 July and 14 July 2004, this witness was granted the pseudonym KV2 and was allowed to testify with facial and voice distortion. May I remind all parties to use the pseudonym at all times during the hearing. Mr. Chief Magistrate, it is necessary, I believe, for you to administer the Australian oath. May I invite you to do so without calling the witness's name. Thank you. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Thank you. Mr. President, I also have an authorisation from the relevant minister of state [inaudible] authorising the taking of such evidence. So I have that here with me. I also have copies of the orders you mentioned dated 25 June 2004. So without further ado, I will arrange to administer an affirmation to the Witness KV2, having called him into court. We're going to just do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief Magistrate. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: We've had the witness outside the courtroom during this part of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. I see. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Yes. Well, the witness is now here. You will be known as KV2. Right. So Mr. KV2, perhaps you could administer the affirmation according to Australian law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Inaudible] CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Chief Magistrate -- CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: We have administered the affirmation. Witness KV2 is now in our witness box and he has the headphones on so he will be able to have the evidence interpreted to him in his own language and his answers in his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Chief Magistrate. Would you have any difficulty if, in order to comply with our own regime here, our representative there were to administer the solemn declaration required by our Rules? CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Not at all. I'll ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: -- of the Tribunal to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: So the oath has been done in the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond witness's own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Magistrate. Now, we have a technical problem of possible disclosure of the name of the witness through the accidental electronic procedures of a videolink conference. I have to confess that I don't myself comprehend these matters exactly. So what I propose is this -- that our representative there is an officer of this Tribunal, and our usher here is also an officer of this Tribunal. So could I ask our representative there to identify himself or herself and to write down the name of the witness on a piece of paper, to show the witness that piece of paper and then to show it to you, Mr. Chief Magistrate. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Yes, go ahead. Madam Registrar's here. Well, I think the witness has been shown his name on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: We will not say it orally. If I can look at it, then we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Yes. Well, I am aware of the witness's name and also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ah, cut off. No transmission. Ah, there we are. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: I will say that again. I was saying I am now aware on this piece of paper of the witness's true name and also his date of birth, and we'll keep that in a closed condition and return it to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now -- CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: For all intents and purposes, now KV2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask the usher here to do likewise, to show the name of the witness -- I don't know what to do. Thank you. Thank you. We had a technical problem which I've solved. So may I ask our usher to show the name of the witness to counsel on both sides and then to the Bench. Now, may I address a further word to the Registrar down there and to the usher here, and that is to say that we are proceeding on the basis that you're both officers of the court and you know the purpose of these proceedings and the identity of the witness to be examined today. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: And I have that indication from the Registrar here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Then, Mr. Chief Magistrate, may I then proceed with some questions which I would put to the witness as a witness of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, in June, July of the year in question, there -- what part of the world did you live in, that is to say, 1992? What part of the world did you live in?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, did anything unusual happen to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean "unusual."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ah. Were you taken anyplace?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the interpreter couldn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would it be possible to have us look at the witness? Make the technicians could be of help at this point. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: I wonder if the witness could keep his voice up because it's got to go all the way back by satellite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We can't see the witness at all. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Are you able to see now, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, Mr. Chief Magistrate. We can't see the witness. I'm sure it will be appreciated -- CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: The technician will work on it at this end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Chief Magistrate, I'm told here that we would need a break of ten minutes in order to direct the cameras to the witness. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: All right. Well, let's have that break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let's have a break. We suspend then for ten minutes to allow for the technicians to do their work. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're suspended at this time. --- Break taken at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. The session stands resumed. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: We will arrange for the witness to be brought into court. He is now coming into court. Are you now able to see the witness, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. No, we're not able -- we're not able to see the witness. We shall resume from where we left off. We will call you Witness KV2. I think you said that in June, July 1992, you lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then -- and I was asking you whether at that time anything unusual happened to you, and you had a problem over the word "unusual," and I corrected myself by explaining that I meant whether you were taking anywhere. Were you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I was taken to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Uh-huh. What was Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Keraterm used to be a ceramics factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What was it at the time when you arrived there? What was it being used for?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: People who were questioned were taken there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then did you remain at Keraterm or did you go somewhere else? Were you taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I only spent two weeks in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't make out the rest of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were you taken anywhere else from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. Two weeks later they took me to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What was Omarska being used for?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: There were other young people who had been taken to Omarska to be questioned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were they taken under arrest?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Did you -- let me show you a sketch model which has been admitted in this -- in these proceedings as Exhibit P3148. You will see it appearing on the screen before you in a few seconds. Tell me when you see it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's answer wasn't audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I don't think the witness gave an answer. Well then, we shall proceed without the sketch. Unless it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, you can see the sketch.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was no audible answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Can that be corrected? Can we get some audibility? We have audibility now? Can you hear me, Witness? I can't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, is the problem being solved?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the technicians in Australia are Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond working to re-establish the volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How is it going there, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're re-establishing the link as we speak, Your Honour. So it will take a few seconds, and we'll see whether the volume is reinstalled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Oh, yes, yes. Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then I was asking you to look at the sketch model which is before you. Does it correspond to anything that you know of?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: There are six squares on the sketch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Do those squares correspond to any building that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I think there's the building where the kitchen was located and the site that was in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were you taken into that building?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: People who were questioned were detained in that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In what room were you taken into?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but it was on a floor. It was upstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If you use this model, would it be A3 or A4 or A1 or A6?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I think were taken up to the floor to be questioned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Right. Now, at Omarska did you see a man called Mr. Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is he alive today?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No, he isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: He died?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: When we were in that house, from that day onwards soldiers cut his throat. We saw the body which was prostrated on the ground in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, would you like to tell us what happened, how his throat was cut?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I can't say the exact date, but when I was in Omarska, we were taken to the house. It was raining on that day. They took in all the people who were outside. I was taken to the "white house" from that building. There were other people in the "white house," people who had been beaten and who were lying on the ground. Then there was some confusion and some fighting between a group of soldiers and people they had taken out of the "white house." Afterwards -- it was a very small house, and there were about 60 people in the house. There were about three small rooms in that "white house." They then brought Mr. Medunjanin, his wife, and his son there. They had previously been beaten. They were bruised. They had bruises on their faces. They then called him out in front of the "white house" and started beating him. Naturally we didn't -- we couldn't watch this, but you could hear him being beaten. Later on, we were to go outside -- when we went outside, we saw his body and a puddle of blood beneath his body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I regret that we have another malfunction. We can now resume. Then -- your last words were that "We -- when we went outside, we saw his body and a puddle of blood beneath his body." Would you like to go on from there.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. There was his corpse in a puddle of blood. The soldiers said that everyone would meet the same fate if they didn't recognise the Serbian army, et cetera, they did not admit to the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us who cut Becir Medunjanin's throat?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I can't tell you the name exactly, but in the group of people who turned up, we weren't allowed to watch what was happening. That's why I can't tell you the exact name, but it was someone in the group of people. These people came with the intention to find this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, when his throat was cut, his head remained attached to his body?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, did you know Mr. Becir Medunjanin previously?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I didn't know him before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Zigic previously? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I saw him while I was in Keraterm for 15 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Did you see a man called Fadil Avdagic -- Avdagic? Perhaps I'm now pronouncing the name correctly. Fadil Avdagic.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. He was also in the "white house."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you one last question. Did you see what happened with Mr. Becir -- Mr. Becir's body? How was it disposed of?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I didn't personally see what happened with the body, but afterwards, after, people went inside to clean everything up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll turn the matter over to counsel. First there would be counsel for Mr. Zigic. Oh, I beg your pardon. Just one moment. Judge Guney has a question or two to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Witness KV2, could you please tell me who was the killer of Becir Medunjanin. Did you see the one who killed him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: As I have already said, I did not personally see the person who killed him, but it was one of the men in the group of soldiers that was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stojanovic, may I invite you to ask any questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could I please be assisted by the interpreter. A name is missing. [In English] "It was one of the men in the group of soldiers that was there." [Interpretation] We don't know who this refers to, so it's missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I believe that is what the witness said, that it was one of the men in the group of soldiers but that he didn't know who it was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness KV2, would you please tell me whether you gave any statements to the Prosecution at some time.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I shall try to simplify the problem since the visual means are imperfect, but I would like to show the witness the statement he gave to the Prosecution, and I will read the last sentence from his statement dated the 22nd of September, 1998. [In English] "I am prepared to come and testify in open court before the International Criminal Tribunal at The Hague, and I am prepared to repeat everything I have stated in my statement." [Interpretation] This is the last sentence in that statement. Do you remember that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the answer -- oh, it's okay now. I can also quote certain passages from that statement, but I'll try to avoid the technical Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond difficulties we are having. You stated very clearly that Duca Knezovic cut off Becir Medunjanin's head, and you were at a distance of one to one and a half metres from that spot.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the "white house" when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg Your Honours for some patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will read also what you said on page 9. [In English] "I know it was raining the day Becir was killed. I saw Zigic in the camp the same afternoon, but after the incident. I'm positive Zigic was not one of the persons participating in the beating and killing of Becir. However, the same day, I saw Zigic call out three or four rich persons and who had their own businesses." [Interpretation] Then you go and mention the names Asef Kapetanovic, et cetera. Do you still stand by what you said then?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, that Zigic did not participate in any way in the killing of Becir Medunjanin, but that he did participate in the beating of some other persons.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I stand by that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was Becir Medunjanin's son present in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, his son was in the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw him, what was happening to him? Can you tell us anything in greater detail about that, what was happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: We didn't see that anything was happening then because we were taken out of the "white house" to the pista very soon after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you said a moment ago, is it correct to say that Zigic was not one of the group of people who took part in the beating and killing of Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: He was not in the "white house," but after that I did see him in Omarska myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [In English] "At the time he was wearing a white shirt and a brown coloured suit. He has -- he had his black shoes on."

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Becir Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I think that is what he was wearing, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I seem to be having problems with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that Becir Medunjanin's son was beaten at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: His wife and his son were brought there one or two nights prior to the father being killed. After, they brought Becir Medunjanin in too, and his son had been beaten before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember anyone else being present in the "white house" either among the people who you found there when you arrived or who came together with you, at the same time as you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Those were mostly people that were brought to the "white house." There was my uncle, who was in Omarska at the same time as me, and myself. He was also in the "white house," of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Abdulah Brkic there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well -- I see. I see. I understand you. Mr. Stojanovic, counsel has drawn your attention to an important element concerning disclosure of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Abdulah Brkic is not a protected witness, whether Fadil Avdagic was there. I just used another name, mentioning Mr. Brkic, who is not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that we just go into closed session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Closed session is ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Azedin Oklopcic, a teacher, a youngish man?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How well do you know Fadil Avdagic, and do you know him at all?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, do you know Zigic?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I didn't know Zigic, but I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you of your statement. I think you said that you had a small shop close to the taxi station and that earlier you would see Zigic quite frequently as a taxi driver there.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: If I saw him, it doesn't mean to say that I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps our language is imperfect in that sense, to know someone. Maybe I should have said would you know his face. I believe you didn't know him personally, but did you know him by sight? Did you know him by sight? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, would you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Simic? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We have no questions either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then I turn to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness KV2, can you see me and hear me quite clearly?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I can hear you and see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were, in 1992, living in Prijedor and a law-abiding citizen who was arrested by armed soldiers who came to your house and took you away, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when the soldiers came, they beat you with iron bars, electric cables, and rifle butts for maybe 15 or 20 minutes, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you were taken from there to the Prijedor Police Station where you were interrogated and forced to sign a statement, a false statement, that you were a member of the Green Berets, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we just move into private session for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Being taken from your house by these armed soldiers and beaten was a terrifying ordeal for you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the police station, apart from being forced to sign a false statement, you were also beaten by being kicked and punched by men with an iron bar, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That too was horrifically terrifying for you because you didn't know what happen, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You spent at least five days in the basement of the police station and during that time the soldiers and police came in every day, sometimes on the hour, to beat you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you moving at this time, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. These are excessively leading questions to the witness, in our submission. I think it was even in the Tadic case that Her Honour Judge McDonald allowed leading, but she said you can lead them but not drag them. And I think these questions are too leading for this occasion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] -- beyond scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, counsel is cross-examining, and I would myself be inclined to feel that we ought to allow him to go a little further.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, I was asking you about your time in the basement at the police station. That was before you were taken to Omarska. You were beaten there on a daily basis by soldiers and the police, and that, too, was an absolutely terrifying ordeal for you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said Omarska. I meant Keraterm, before you were taken to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you arrived at Keraterm, the people there took all your valuables from you.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers took everything away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were imprisoned in what could only be described as horrific conditions. You were fed maybe once every 24 to 48 hours and only fed one slice of bread per day on some days, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Counsel, do you think it might be possible for you to apply a little restraint to those questions. There is something in what Mr. Stojanovic said, that you may lead the witness but not drag the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm attempting to do this as quickly as possible. There is a route I'm going, and it will take me a lot longer if I ask open-ended questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but can you try. An objection has been taken on the other side. I have sought in my own way to allow you to proceed, but not too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, the point I'm -- the point about this is you were confined in horrific conditions in Keraterm and not properly fed, not provided with proper sanitation, and at the same time people were being beaten and murdered while you were there.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And just like your experience in the police station, this was an horrific, terrifying ordeal for you and all the other people contain at Keraterm, wasn't it? And you didn't know whether you would live or die from day to day, did you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After this, just if I were to observe this on the side, I would get the impression that Mr. Re is more familiar with the mental state of the witness than the witness himself. So I really think that is beyond the scope -- with all due respect in the Anglo-Saxon system that allows for leading questions -- but I think this is going a bit too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Re -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in any event, it is beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I suggest that some attention be given to the objection being made, which is if I may translate it this way, that there is a distinction between a leading question in cross-examination and counsel giving the evidence himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, when you were at Keraterm and at Omarska, were names called from a list of people, and were people taken away? Some came back and were beaten, and others just disappeared. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was that a terrifying thing for you and everyone else there?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Of course it was, because one never knew when your turn could come.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that the same when you were put on the bus to Omarska? Did you think your turn could have come when you were put on the bus to Omarska, and you could have been taken out and been killed? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That was the first thing that crossed my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were at Omarska, were the conditions of confinement similar to those at Keraterm, that is the lack of food, sanitation, and cramped conditions for sleeping?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see a person called Rizo Hadzalic die from a particularly horrific beating while you were at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the pista at the time. And we heard him being beaten just because of a word that he had used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I saw Mr. Fila on his legs. I don't know whether you wanted to move a motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, during the trial proceedings in this case, the Chamber introduced a rule that the cross-examination may not go beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief. That is how we have defended our clients over the past three years. If you said that it is important in this case to examine the witness to establish the role of Zoran Zigic in the killing of Becir Medunjanin, in your ruling you have actually limited his testimony to one particular event, and that is whether Zoran Zigic has anything to do with the killing of Medunjanin. And the witness said he didn't, and that was the examination-in-chief. And that is how we acted throughout the defence of our clients. That was a rule introduced by Judge Rodrigues. Now we're listening about the police station in Prijedor, about Keraterm and Omarska. That is a renewed examination-in-chief. So that is my objection. The Prosecution can only focus on the relationship between Zigic and Medunjanin and nothing beyond that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is directed to the witness's state of mind at the time he witnessed it and when he made his statement. I'm not opening up other areas. And I have finished with that, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, you have finished. Mr. Re has finished up with that aspect, so perhaps we might allow him to proceed to another branch of his inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. KV2, could I just summarise: When you left Omarska -- by the time you left Omarska, you had lost a considerable amount of weight. Is that as a result of the basically starvation rations you were fed there?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would it be fair -- I don't want to put words in your mouth, would you would it be fair to say that you were psychologically traumatised by your experiences at the Prijedor Police Station, Keraterm, and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you witness a number of incidents of people being beaten and killed at Keraterm and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I can't say that I personally witnessed this, but I saw that there were people who were lying on the ground who had been beaten, who -- who were bleeding. I can't say that I was personally present when they did these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Re, is it your position that this is also directed to the state of mind of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what he saw; yes, both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thought you had passed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I asked him whether he'd seen people being beaten and killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. I thought you had passed that part of the inquiry directed to the state of mind of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I had. That's why I asked him whether he'd seen people being killed. That's the subject, I understand, of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But I thought you had passed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm moving to the specific incident for which we are here. I'm sorry if there's any confusion. I'm directly on Mr. Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, did you know Becir Medunjanin before you went to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know his son or his wife before you went to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you confined when you were at Omarska? Where were you kept or where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: At the beginning, we were at the -- I was at the pista. That's where we would spend the day, and in the evening we slept elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Becir Medunjanin? Were you ever introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No, I was never introduced to him. He'd been taken two days and he wasn't there for long.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you only know his name because other people told you that a person who had been killed there's name was Becir Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I heard his name when we were in the "white house." When soldiers called his name out, we knew that it was his name, because he responded to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And to make this clear, did you actually see this person leaving the "white house"? Or you assumed that he had left the "white house" when the soldiers called out that name?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: You're referring to Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. They called his name out, he and went out with that group of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To make this perfectly clear, you remained inside the "white house," and this person you say was Becir Medunjanin was taken outside, that is outside the building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No, not outside the room. He was called out. He responded, and they started beating him immediately in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is it the situation that you could only hear but not see what was happening outside the room you were in?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. We heard him being beaten, and we heard him crying out when Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond he was being beaten. They ordered us to face the wall, not to watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you said in response to His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen's questions earlier that you saw the body outside, are we to take it to mean that you were talking about outside the "white house," outside the building?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No. I wanted to say that it was in the hall, because there was a small hall, and there were three small rooms in that building, in the "white house." Afterwards, they made us go out, after everything that had happened, and we passed by the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say you passed by the body, are you saying -- is this what happened? You heard the sounds of beating outside. The soldiers left, and then you went outside and there was a body in the hallway or corridor.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: First they called him out. This -- we didn't see what was happening, but we saw the body and a puddle of blood.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter didn't catch the full answer. There was some interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, can you just please repeat what you said? We got up to "We didn't see what was happening, but we saw the body and a puddle of blood." Did you say something after that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: We heard them calling him out, and we heard them beating him. And he started crying out. And afterwards, when they were driving us out of the "white house," we saw the body lying in a puddle of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: In the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- to the Appeals Chamber that you did not see anyone do anything to the body which was in the puddle of blood; that is, the soldiers or guards had left by then and the body was just lying there by itself?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: That's not way wanted to say, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to clarify, Mr. KV2. When you saw the body, was there anyone around the body or did you just walk past it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: There was a group of soldiers, the group that drove us out of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were these soldiers and what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: We were at the entrance. They were in the hallway by the body. They insulted us, and they drove us out of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying you then left the "white house," leaving the soldiers behind with the body?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you walk straight from the "white house" somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: We all went to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were on the pista, did you look back into the "white house" or were you concerned with other things?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No, we couldn't look at other things because they told us to turn our faces towards the asphalt, and not to watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say you saw the body lying in a pool of blood, were you assuming that he had had some part of his body cut which had caused the pool of blood to form?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Naturally. While I was going out, I saw that there was a wound from which the person was bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You saw the wound. Are you telling the Trial Chamber [sic] you didn't actually see anyone inflict the wound upon the body? But assumed because there had been people outside, sound of beatings, that the people doing the beating must have wounded him?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said there was a wound in the neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And are you also telling the Appeals Chamber that you didn't see the body after that? The last time you saw the body was when it was lying in a pool of blood in the corridor in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you ever spoken to Becir Medunjanin's son? Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No. I haven't spoken to his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: About how many people were in the "white house" on that day when you heard this beating, the sounds of beating in the corridor and you had your back to the -- you had your face to the wall?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: As it was raining, there were a lot of people. There were only people who had been punished in that house, but as it was raining, they'd all taken shelter in the room. There were about 60 people at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were there people between you and the door when you were standing there with your -- facing the wall?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: There were a lot of people around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there people between you and the door, the door leading to the corridor?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was the effect of the people being in the room to muffle the sounds of whatever was happening in the corridor outside?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: One could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because you were standing with your face to the wall away from the beating in the corridor outside, you aren't able to tell the Appeals Chamber, are you, who was in the corridor doing the beating? The situation is you just don't know, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I can't say exactly who was there from that group of people. Someone beat him from that group of people, but you can't say who exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because if you were standing in the room facing the wall and there were other people between you and the door, other people could have come into the corridor from the "white house" and beat the person without you knowing, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Dr. Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Dr. Sadikovic was in the "white house" on that day or was with you on the pista on that day? If you don't remember, please just say so.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I think he was in the "white house" on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say you think, is it based upon the fact that there were a lot of people there and you had seen him around and he may or may not have been there, but that he was just one of the people who was around?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Mr. Sadikovic, I saw him taken -- he was taken there about seven days before the event happened, and he was placed in the house. Afterwards, they didn't leave the "white house." They put us in the "white house" afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to say now, 12 years after the event, whether Mr. Medunjanin's son was in the room with you when this happened? That is, when you were facing the wall, there were all these people crowded in the room, and someone was being beaten in the corridor outside.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, when you ask me whether this is something I could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it must have been some confusion here. I'm asking you whether you remember now, 12 years after this terrible day, whether Mr. Medunjanin's son was in that room with you.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I remember he and his mother were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether they stayed in the room with you while this beating was occurring outside?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I think they were in the first room, since people were kept separately in the first room. We weren't kept in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying you think they were there and you think they were in a different room?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: They were in that room on the left in the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that the same room you were in or a different room?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: It was a different room, since we were in the two other small Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you're saying this now, are you saying you think that they were there in this different room when you were in the other room with your face to the wall crowded in with a lot of people while the beating was occurring?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the witness has already answered this question twice. It's not necessary to repeat it, especially given the leading nature of the questions. And this is the third time that this has happened. The questions put are excessively leading. The witness has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. I don't think we have a picture, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question is directed to a different room, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. I'm saying I don't think we have a picture on the screen. You were explaining that the question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Oh. There's no transmission at the moment. Just to respond to my learned friend's objection. I'm not leading. I'm saying do you think they were in the different room, that is asking him, giving him the chance to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's necessary for me to say that the two previous answers -- answers to the question, it's not just a matter of leading questions, but a few lines before the witness already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, in the circumstances, we propose to suspend for 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Mr. President, we're going to bring the witness back into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Splendid, Mr. Magistrate. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: We're ready to proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Re, I had -- I had computed that you had seven minutes more to go. Would that be agreeable for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thought it was ten, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ten minutes. So let it be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we need to make an observation. Our examination of the witness -- and you say that this is a Court witness, but it was our suggestion that he be heard, and we requested a subpoena. The Chamber agreed with our suggestion and agreed to organise this testimony, and we're not entitled to re-examination. Our examination-in-chief is more limited because we are not allowed to ask any leading questions, took ten minutes. On the other hand, the Prosecution is allowed excessive cross-examination. He is given much greater possibilities for their questions, and we feel that this is quite in contrast with the policy of equal arms. So could the Chamber please take note of the fact that the Defence feels that they are being treated unfairly in this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. We'll see what we can do to facilitate you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just note that the Scheduling Order says for all counsel examination for the same period, Mr. Stojanovic included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Re, we are extending your time by three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, you made a statement to the -- to investigators and lawyers from the Office of the Prosecutor on the 21st and 22nd of September, 1998. Do you have a copy of at that statement there with you at the moment? CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Mr. President, it may assist counsel for the Prosecution, we have an English statement here only, but certainly no translated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would that be of any help to you, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I understand it was taken in English, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, you have your statement there in English. You read and understand English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I have the statement, but I don't read English.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, I'll read you a passage from paragraph -- sorry, page 8 of the statement. Do you remember making the statement in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In the statement you said: "As soon as they stopped beating him," that's meaning Becir, "I saw Duca who was facing my direction, pull out his military knife from his right-hand sheath. I have served in the military and know what military knife looks like. I noticed the blade was 27 centimetres long. Becir's body was between me and Duca. As soon as he took his knife out, Duca bent down and completely decapitated Becir's head from the rest of the body." That's what you told the OTP investigator and lawyer in September 1998, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I don't remember saying it to him like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You then go on saying -- "He then took out his knife --" I'm sorry. You then go on to say: "When the head was cut off --" I'm sorry. I will withdraw that. What I've just read to you from your statement is different from the testimony you gave today to the Appeals Chamber, isn't it? Because you told the Appeals Chamber earlier you didn't see how Mr. Medunjanin was injured.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: In my first statement I also said what I saw, and never did I mention the name of the person who might have done it. I just said there was a group of people and that I know that it was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The statement then goes on: "When the head was cut off, I remember the body was still shaking. After severing the head, Saponja and the other guards started to kick the head. I believe they kicked the head nine to ten times, and Saponja, then looking at us, said, 'Each one of you who has participated in anything he did will end up like him.' Duca did not kick the head. He was totally covered in blood." That's what your statement to the OTP investigator and lawyer taken in September 1998 says. That, sir, is of course very different to the evidence you gave today, that you did not see what happened to the body, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I didn't say that I didn't see what happened to the body. We saw the body lying in a pool of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, you certainly didn't see anyone decapitate the head and then the guards kick it around like a football, did you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I saw a body lying and -- that had a cut on the throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, you have a copy of the statement there in English. I don't want to see the front cover so that it identifies who you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Perhaps the Chief Magistrate might be able to assist us here or the registry officer will help us in Australia with the document. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: The registrar will do it. The witness now has before him a statement in English, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief Magistrate. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Now, what is it you wish us to do with that statement, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm in the hands of counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Chief Magistrate, I'm in the hands of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I wish the Chief Magistrate just to identify, looking at the statement, that it does in fact bear the witness's name so that he can identify that particular statement has the witness's name on the front. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: I'll do that now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And then I'll ask the witness to look at the signature. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: I confirm, Mr. President, that the witness statement does have his name on the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Chief Magistrate. Yes, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, can you just please look at the statement. It's a seven-page statement -- or eight-page statement. I just want you to -- 13-page statement. I apologise. It's a 13-page statement. I want you just to identify that that is in fact a statement that you have signed, that has been taken by the OTP -- sorry, Prosecution investigators, and that you have signed the front page and initialed each of the bottom of the pages and signed an acknowledgement at the end, on page 14.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, I have this statement, and there is -- in the middle there are two pages that are not signed at the bottom that seem to have been added.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What page numbers are those?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: There's no number on those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this your statement dated the 21st and 22nd of September, 1998?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Perhaps, Mr. President, I could check the statement and endeavour to just corroborate what the witness has said about numbers on the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief Magistrate. I'm looking at my --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief Magistrate. I'm looking at my copy, and I don't see the deficiency averted to by the witness. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: I'll just examine the statement myself. The registrar informed me that this is the copy she received from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, I'm just trying to find out if you have the same document there. Are there 14 pages? It's a statement dated the 21st and 22nd of September, 1998. Thirteen pages with the one-page back sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The trouble, Mr. Re, is that we -- the trouble is that we're running out of time, are we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want the witness to identify it and then tender it for the purposes of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay. I won't take up any time. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Mr. President, can I just confirm that the pages bearing the serial numbers 00642184, 00642185 are two pages that don't have enumerated numbers, and they don't have initials on them either. All the other pages appear to be enumerated and initialed. Those two pages do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief Magistrate. My copy is different, then. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: I've referred to the typed numbers on the top right-hand corner in identifying the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: There are also numbers 1 to 13 on the bottom, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's possible by faxing or something or copying, because it bears the same ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me find out from Mr. Re what he is interested in. Are you interested in the signatures at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could confirm that that is indeed -- the witness has made the statement and signed it. It would appear explicable that some pages may not bear the bottom part from maybe a copying process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But your interest is in the signatures at the bottom of the page? I gather that the witness is a saying that there are two pages which do not have any signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are, but those two pages have the numbers at the top. It would appear that when they have been copied or faxed, the bottom two -- the bottom part which has got the number and initials hasn't come through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are those two pages relevant to what you're asking the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, then can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- on that basis? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. KV2, that is the statement that you made, and apart from those two pages - I think it was 4 and 5 - they all bear your initials on the bottom, and it bears your signature at the end and at the front; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is in fact the statement that you made to the investigators or lawyers, and it was read back to you in Bosnian and you signed the English, is that correct, on the 22nd of September, 1998?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Will that be all, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That is all. And there is one question I wish to ask him in closed session, and that is everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Closed session ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And while that's being done, may I tender this statement on the appeal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That concludes my cross-examination, and I move to tender the witness's statement of 21st and 22nd of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Those pages which bear his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, the entirety of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: With the exception of those two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, with the entirety of the document. They run sequentially. It just appears the two that aren't particularly relevant haven't come through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well now, Mr. Re, we had taken account of Mr. Stojanovic's representations, and we would now give him ten minutes. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, though according to the Scheduling Order I had not expected to be given this chance, but in any event, I'm very grateful for being given this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. KV2, did the Prosecution take any other statements from you prior to 1998?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution first compile a statement including many things that you never said?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I was given that statement because I was visited by a gentleman without an interpreter when I arrived in the country, and he compiled a statement that he took with him. And then when they came in 1998, I saw that this was the statement which I hadn't really compiled or given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in that first statement of 1995 the investigators of the Prosecution mentioned many things that you hadn't said and that were not correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: They mentioned many things; that is, many things that I had allegedly seen but which I hadn't seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that first statement, was it stated, for instance, that Zigic had beaten you up, whereas you hadn't said that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I really don't remember exactly what that statement of 1995 really looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many times have you actually been in contact with the OTP of the Tribunal, altogether.

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I was visited twice, one in 1995 and one in 1998. They came to my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Didn't they come several times in 1995 to see you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No. They came once. The first day they wrote the statement and the second day they just came for me to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how many times has the Defence been in contact with you, including myself and Zigic or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I have not had contact with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen or heard me in your life?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I not mistaken, in this statement you also mention a certain Hajra Hadzic in the "white house." What can you tell us about her?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: At the beginning, she was detained in the "white house" too. And she stayed there when a group of 174 men stayed behind. I was one of them, and there were four women. That was the period when the camp was being disbanded. We were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Becir Medunjanin's wife in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Could you explain what period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of the incident in the "white house" when Becir was killed, was she there?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: When he was killed she was there, but later on she was taken upstairs to the rooms where the other women were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clearly hear the voices of the people who were beating up and who killed Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: We could hear the voices of the soldiers who were insulting and cursing, but most of all the moans of the person who was being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the group of soldiers when they left the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: The group of soldiers who did that stayed in the "white house." We left the "white house," and we went off to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you pass by them in the corridor in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Of course we passed by the soldiers as we were leaving the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you then see Zigic amongst them?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I can not say I saw him, because we had our heads about -- you must understand that no one dared look or ask anything at all in that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I take it that you are about to wind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But how far were you from those soldiers when you passed them?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: The corridor is very narrow, and we were leaving in a line, one by one, to go through the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have touched them with your hand?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: Of course I could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me inquire from Mr. Fila, Mr. Simic. No questions. Let me turn to my colleagues on the Bench. One question from Judge Guney. I shouldn't say one question. Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Witness KV2, I want you to clarify one point. You may recall the statement that you made on the 21st of August, 1995, before the representative of the Prosecutor. In that statement, in paragraph 5, you say, and I quote: "I saw Becir Medunjanin being killed by Duca with an electric cable and baton. Becir died in our room. Duca had slit his throat." Is it correct? Is this statement correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: The statement that I signed in 1995, naturally someone came from The Hague. He didn't leave a visit card of any kind so that I could know that he was the man in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Because today -- or when I put to you the question who was the killer of Becir Medunjanin, you said you didn't know that. How do you consider this is true statement?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: In 1995 when I gave that statement, my knowledge of English was very poor. Naturally I tried to explain things to him, but I never mentioned any names. I never said that such-and-such a person had done something. I said that there was a group of people, but I never mentioned the name of one individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: So you didn't -- you didn't mention the name of Duca during your statement?

utterances.speaker: Witness KV2
utterances.text: I did mention his name. I said that he was in the group of men who went to the "white house."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness KV2. I don't think there are any more questions. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I address the Chief Magistrate to say that this Bench of the Appeals Chamber thanks the authorities in the Commonwealth of Australia for their kind cooperation in helping to make these arrangements. And we thank you, Chief Magistrate, very especially for participating in our ongoing effort to administer international criminal justice. CHIEF MAGISTRATE CAHILL: Thank you, Mr. President. It has been our pleasure to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Well, on that note, we will adjourn the proceedings until tomorrow for another videolink conference. Is that right? Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of July, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [The appellant Kvocka not present in court]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.55 p.m.,
